newsitem.title: USA: CBOT wheat ends lower on USDA carryover, soybeans.
newsitem.headline: CBOT wheat ends lower on USDA carryover, soybeans.

text.p: CBOT wheat futures closed lower on a collapse in soybean futures plus bearishness stemming from USDA's projection for 1996-97 U.S. wheat carryover at 465 million bushels, traders said.
Analysts had expected the government to place the carryover at roughly 450 million bushels.
"For quite awhile wheat and corn were supported by old crop beans and when beans broke it hit wheat and corn," said Joel Karlin, senior grains Analyst for Chicag-based Everen Securities.
USDA's wheat production estimates also was bearish.
USDA estimated 1997 U.S. wheat production at 2.261 billion bushels which was about in line with trade expectations and did little to generate demand for futures.
"USDA is saying with any normal weather the supply/demand situation is going to be a lot different than it was the past two years," Karlin said.
Record high prices were set roughly a year ago in wheat and corn futures on projections for low carryover of each.
Wheat futures closed two to 14-3/4 cents per bushel lower, with May down 12 cents at $3.93 per bushel. New crop July was 14-3/4 cents lower at $3.99.
Traders said there were no surprises in USDA's outlook for U.S. winter wheat production at 1.561 billion bushels.

That estimated tally was six percent above last year's output of 1.478 billion. A mid-April freeze cut into hard red winter wheat production prospects but not as much as some in the market had expected.
USDA said hard red winter production in 1997 would total 893.927 million bushels, above 762.402 million bushels produced in 1996.
Wheat also was hit by USDA's weekly export inspections report.
Drier-than-desired wheat conditions in western Kansas underpinned the market and USDA's weekly export inspections report was neutral for wheat futures.
USDA Monday said U.S. wheat inspected for export during the week ended May 8 totaled 12.836 million bushels, within the range of expectations for nine million to 14.0 million bushels.
USA Trading sold two million bushels of July and Merrill Lynch Futures sold 1.8 million July, traders said. Cargill Inc bought three million bushels of July, traders said.
Wheat futures volume was estimated by the CBOT at 20,000 contracts, above the 11,995 contracts traded Friday.
Options-related selling also hit wheat futures, traders said.

FIMAT Futures bought 2,000 July $4.20 puts and sold 2,000 September $4.10 puts at even money to two cents, traders said. FIMAT also bought 2,000 July $4.10 puts and sold 2,000 September $4.00 puts at 1-1/2 to 1-1/4 cents, traders said.
Wheat options volume was estimated at 10,000 contracts, above the 7,528 traded Friday.

On Monday afternoon after the market closed, USDA said 53 percent of U.S. winter wheat as of Sunday was in good to excellent condition. That was an improvement from 28 percent of wheat in that category the previous week. Also, USDA said 47 percent of winter wheat was in very poor to poor condition, less than 72 percent in that category the previous week which was also an improvement.
